full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll start off telling you a bit about what we're doing, so the bigger picture makes sense to you. We're looking at women engineering students' first experience of the workplace (uh huh) and we're seeing what impact it has on their career (right) which is mainly why we want to interview people that are going on placement, but we're also asking questions about the first educational experiences of engineering and expectations, and also why women have chosen not to go on placement or aren't going on placement, so that's why we wanted some non-placement students. And at the end of the project we're going to put some guidelines together and we'll give them back to the engineering industry. So I'll start off just asking you about some background questions and about why you wanted to do engineering – is it civil engineering you're doing?

Subject:	I'm trying to.

Interviewer:	Are you doing the Masters course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	What A levels did you do?

Subject:	Erm, I did general studies, German, and maths and physics.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Now you're asking. It was a – it's got a special name and I can't remember. It was basically a local comprehensive but it's an ecumenical school with a church entry requirement.

Interviewer:	Right OK

Subject:	But it's 11 to 18.

Interviewer:	Boys and girls?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm I did do 3 months with [company] in [town] but that was at the end of my first year.

Interviewer:	OK, Are either of your parents engineers?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	So when and why do you think that you decided to study engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I was originally interested in geo physics, erm sort of working with volcanoes or earthquakes but because geo physics has a very narrow qualification I decided that civil engineering would be better. Because – although it would allow me to do geo physics if I wanted to – you know I could specialise in that, it would also enable me to take on other jobs if, you know, over the 4 years, I decided that I wanted to do something else.

Interviewer:	OK did you decide to do engineering before you chose your A levels, or after?

Subject:	After.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide which 'A' levels to do?

Subject:	Erm, well it was based on the subjects I found interesting and that I was good at.

Interviewer:	OK did anything else influence your decision to study engineering, like parents or anything in the media, or careers advice – anything like that?

Subject:	Probably my mum because my uncle studied civil engineering and so I think my mum originally suggested it, because I hadn't really heard much about engineering. It was sort of something that existed in the sub-conscious somewhere – you don't really actively think about it.

Interviewer:	Yeah – did you do much career research then?

Subject:	Oh my goodness, I did an awful lot but I can't say engineering ever came up.

Interviewer:	OK, did you talk to your uncle about engineering then – did he encourage you or discourage you at all?

Subject:	Well, my uncle did a BEng in civil engineering and then went into the finance world. So I didn't really talk to him about it no.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider doing any of the other types of engineering?

Subject:	Erm, yes, I applied for both aero and civil but I decided to go with civil because I dec – well, aero has an element of electronics in it and I cannot do electronics. And in the end I decided that civils was probably more diverse and that I would find it more interesting in the long run.

Interviewer:	OK, that's great, how did you decide to come to [university]?

Subject:	Erm, well my maths teacher came here and that was the first I'd heard about it. Mm, it – my choice was really between [this university] or [university 2], because they both have very good civil engineering and aero eng departments. And, in the end I decided [this university], because I came here for a visit and it was friendly – [university]. And yeah, [university 2] actually has got a big hill, so you've got the halls of residence on the top and the civil engineering department at the bottom and I just really didn't fancy that.

Interviewer:	I don't blame you! When you decided to do civil engineering then, did you realise it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Oh yeah.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	No, I mean my maths 'A' level was – well the mechanics group it was 9 boys and me – so, it didn't really phase me at all and a lot of my friends are male.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to be engineers?

Subject:	Yes. I think – well, I felt that – you know – it wasn't really given to me as an option when I was at school. I knew virtually nothing about it. And I don't know what the case was for the boys – you know, maybe they knew about it – just sort of intuitively or something, er but certainly you know, it wasn't flagged up as something I could do.

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done? How do you think they could go about encouraging more women, or making more women aware?

Subject:	I'm not sure (laughs). I've erm, I belong, I've joined WES, you know, I'm sort of doing the – what is it? – the e-mentoring scheme, with the local schools and I think that's probably quite a good way because the girls have teamed up with one us university students and you know, although it's actually just sort of – almost a friendship via email – you know, they can ask you questions about university and about engineering specifically. And they are sort of between 11 and 14 I think. So that's quite an early age but not too early to make them aware that there is this thing called engineering out there. Which is a good thing – but obviously that's only – that only reaches a very small number of people. You know, probably the best thing would be to address 'A' level students who are doing maths and/or physics. Or just general careers sense.

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	What sort of an engineer?

Interviewer:	Oh a civil engineer.

Subject:	A civil engineer. Erm, ability to work in mud (laughter). You've got to be determined and, to get anywhere, you need to be ambitious. So you have to – even when you've finished university – you have to carry on working towards your chartered status, so you need to be willing to put in the extra work that's required and not expect a 9 to 5 job. So if you want to rise in the company, you need to put in probably about 110%. You know, so people can see you're there, see you're dedicated and that you're making the effort. Erm, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male ones – in there?

Subject:	Mm, no because women that choose to go into engineering usually know what they're up against and whereas men appear to sort of drift into engineering for lack of anything else to do, women actually choose to do engineering and will only do – you know they know they're good at it and its something they're interested in. So in a strange way, those characteristics possibly apply more to women than men.

Interviewer:	OK, Do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a female engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I think it's a disadvantage when you're starting out, because like it or not, many men are still prejudiced and you know, although they'll have women in their working team and they'll be used to working with them, when a new woman turns up – you know – it's a case of sort of getting to know them and until you know the way they do the job, they're sort of possibly more on probation than the men would be. And you're sort of – well, when I was working anyway, I felt I had to put in extra effort above and beyond what I was actually asked to do – you know – in order to be accepted. And I'm not sure that would apply to men. But then, later on, you know if you're a manager, as a woman, and your team happen to be men, then you've got an awful lot of control because women are probably more manipulative – aren't they? You can probably get them to do more, than if there was a male on the job.

Interviewer:	Yes. So – but you think it's harder for them to get into that position in the first place?

Subject:	Yes. Well, not least because you cannot be an engineer and have a family – it just doesn't work.

Interviewer:	Does that worry you at all?

Subject:	Well, I'm not going to be an engineer.

Interviewer:	OK, we'll talk about that later. Has the degree been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	In as far as I expected anything, yes, it's always hard work. I don't think I really had any firm expectations before I came. I'd read the course content and I knew vaguely what we would be attacking but erm….

Interviewer:	What about in terms of the gender proportions or the type of teaching that you've had?

Subject:	The teaching's been very good – actually with probably one or two exceptions. The teaching has been excellent. Gender proportions are fine – it just doesn't fuss me at all.

Interviewer:	How many women are on your course?

Subject:	Erm, in this year er I think 10 women and 64 in total, so 54 men. And from my other year, I think there were only 5 women and 70 men – that was when we started, I think since then a few have dropped out but…

Interviewer:	OK. What has been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, I'm not sure really. The best thing is getting course work in on time – in civil engineering we don't have any choice – we have to hand it in otherwise it doesn't get accepted.. The worst thing has got to be the sheer volume of work at times, and the fact that you sort of start a week and finish a week without having actually seen daylight, because you're glued to your desk.

Interviewer:	Do you think that, that helps you – although it's not nice at times, compared to other students doing other subjects, that, that might prepare you for when you do go into the industry?

Subject:	Erm, possibly. I was speaking to civil engineers who are out in industry. Very few of them work in the same way they did when they were students. In fact, hardly any. You know, mostly they're doing a range different things but you're not – you're not working as hard as you were – I mean at university – so in a way, we are prepared. You know we'll go out and suddenly work will be easy but at the same time there's a chance that you sort of feel that – you know – why do we work so hard – what's the point if in actual fact, you're never going to touch hydraulics again! Why did you spend2 years of your life learning it. It's just – it's just one of those things because civil engineering' so broad.

Interviewer:	OK, Are you pleased that you chose to do this course?

Subject:	I think so. I didn't want something that was all very samey. I wanted something that was quite diverse. Something that would interest me as much as possible.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	One.

Interviewer:	Did you think that they had a different style to male lecturers?

Subject:	Well, the problem is she's not strictly engineering – she's more sort of computers or something or another and it's quite difficult because she sets you – she sets her course work which was requiring that you use your engineering knowledge, and yet she herself didn't seem to know what it was that we were looking for, when we came to ask her questions. And – which makes it quite difficult. She's very organised but then again so is all the men but er…

Interviewer:	Did you think that the female lecturer treated you any differently to the male lecturers?

Subject:	Not really because we don't have that much individual contact with lecturers, unless, you know, we're going to ask for help and I think everybody just gets treated the same. I don't think there is any noticeable difference. We're all students when it comes down to it.

Interviewer:	That's OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you at all? Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	Not really. No it doesn't bother me at all that I've got a male personal tutor. I get on really well with him and so on. You know, he sort of keeps up to date with what I'm doing, which is great. But no, it hadn't even occurred to me that I might want a female personal tutor.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Is there anything or anyone that you'd say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Is that in academic terms or…?

Interviewer:	Yeah, or even … ?

Subject:	Erm, in academic terms I don't know – I think friends who are interested in the same thing, who are doing the same piece of work – has been very motivating, because when you get stuck there's always some people to talk to. 

Interviewer:	No, that's fine. Has the type of teaching that you've had involved much group work?

Subject:	As in course work groups or labs?

Interviewer:	Both, yeah.

Subject:	Well we do erm lab work – that's all done in groups. Erm, that's been quite significant amount of work. And then we also have group work, which is course work which to be submitted in groups.

Interviewer:	OK, when you work in groups, how do you decide who you're going to work with?

Subject:	Erm, well, there's people that you know and people you know complement your skills, generally when you've got a choice. Lab groups are allocated – so you just do the best you can within that.

Interviewer:	Do you tend to work with males or females or doesn't it bother you either way?

Subject:	It doesn't bother me either way. Erm, it just so happened that my lab group was 3 males and in other group work I've been with like another girl and 2 males. Erm, …

Interviewer:	Do you think that males and females bring different skills to group work?

Subject:	No. No, the skills are purely dictated by what personality and the ability of the person, to be honest.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Yeah. (laughter)

Interviewer:	What?

Subject:	You want the details? (yeah) Right, well I worked in a group with 2 of my friends – 2 males, 1 female and it just so happened that I had a personality clash with one of my friends, which we hadn't realised before because it doesn't come into conflict – but we're both leadership types and it was a male, which wasn't a problem but you know, it just so happened, and he was unable to recognise what was going on and to deal with it. So his attitude was to just ride over the top of it. So I decided that as he obviously didn't have a clue, I would take a back seat and just get on with the work. And then it happened that this guy and the girl – they were both working on it, when the other two of us weren't around and they were making decisions. And then, you know, we would find out 'oh by the way we've done this', which wasn't really helpful in a group situation. So basically communication was non-existent and I was left out – you know – in one way or another. You know, they wouldn't tell me there was a group meeting or they'd say, 'oh we've organised a group meeting for Tuesday. Are you around?' And I wouldn't be, because I'd previously arranged something. Anyway, went it came to it, it was peer assessed. They'd marked me right down, which you know, I felt was completely unfair because within the boundaries, that they'd virtually placed on me, I'd done the best I could, you know I'd contributed in all areas, I'd done as much work as I could but they – and the girl and the guy who were being basically control freaks, weren't allocating the work really. They were wanting to do everything themselves. So I came out with a bad mark, compared to the others. That wasn't brilliant.

Interviewer:	What do you think you'd do if that situation occurred again?

Subject:	Well that situation is occurring again, because I'm working with this group for my field course that's coming up, but I think it will be fine because I did speak to them about what was going on and you know, I raised my concerns with them and hopefully now, we'll just settle down to some sort of working pattern and it should be fine.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the benefits or the advantages and disadvantages of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, well the advantages have got to be that when you go out into industry, everything's group work. You're very, very unlikely to do anything by yourself. And you know, invariably you will have to refer to somebody else or gather some information that somebody else has collected and talk with them about what happens. Erm, so it's a very good thing to be doing group work, at this stage, because you learn how to get along when – you know – things aren't quite right and you learn what you have to do, in order to rectify the situation. And disadvantages? There aren't really any I don't think

Interviewer:	OK, how have you decided not to go on a placement – because you were considering … ?

Subject:	Yes, I was going to go on a placement. Originally when I started university I was sponsored. (OK) But, I got ill and I had to take 7 months leave of absence in my original 2nd year. So I did 3 months of my 2nd year and then I had to leave because I was ill. And at which point, they terminated my sponsorship – erm, all well and good. Erm, so then when I came back, I had to apply to other companies – which has been fine but I'm restricted because of my husband's – he's doing a PhD and I can't – well I don't really want to live outside of the country – I want to commute every week and I just haven't been able to find a job in the area. So I've decided that I'm better off going straight through and then just getting out into industry one year earlier.

Interviewer:	Yeah. When you did your 3 months, previously, was that with the sponsored company?

Subject:	Yes it was.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of going on a placement then?

Subject:	Industrial placement?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Erm, I think the advantages are that you see what you've been learning, sort of being employed and you – you sort of see how – the sort of work when you leave university, because they basically treat you like a graduate and you assume responsibilities in line with your capability. And er that's a good thing because it makes you motivated to come back, learn the extra bit and then get out there and you know, if that's what you want to do. Or, you know it might show you that actually you don't want to do engineering and that you'd be better off finishing off and you know, doing something else. So it's just like a form of taster of what life will be like after Uni.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like the 3 months experience that you have had went some way in doing that?

Subject:	Er, it helped discourage me.

Interviewer:	Did it? Why?

Subject:	Erm, well I was placed between 2 teams – geotechnics and transportation and erm the guy in charge of transportation, for whatever reason, just didn't like me and he made my life a misery – quite literally. And in the end he accused of me lying and I was rather upset by that shall we say and then they moved me to geotechnics and then everything was fine – you know, I really enjoyed that. But, I think the few weeks that I had with transportation was an absolute misery.

Interviewer:	Did you think that was to do with being a woman or just a personality thing?

Subject:	No, I was just a student – you know I didn't know what I was doing – he could pick on me, which he did.

Interviewer:	Just inexperience.

Subject:	Yeah, and he'd accused me of revising while I was at work, which anybody who knows me, will tell you that's very unlikely. You know, I'd brought my revision books with me, because I'd revised to and from work, on the train. Erm, but I didn't ever touch them while I was – really I just ,,,

Interviewer:	OK, what were the best things about that experience then?

Subject:	Erm, being given things to do – where you start off actually not knowing what's going on, but then, by the end of it, erm you know you're competent in doing that. So in my case I learnt 2 different things – I learnt how to set up a programme that basically simulated roundabouts and traffic junctions and I designed the junction and input it. And it involved learning how the programme worked, which was great because, you know, you could see the end product and what the traffic jams were going to be like. Erm, and then with geotechnics I had to write up a report on erm an airfield they were going to build on, which involves us sort of analysing ground surveys and (?) and various things (OK) That was interesting. Yeah, it's also proving useful now I'm doing geotechnics because we use the same sorts of things.

Interviewer:	When you was in the transport department, would you have enjoyed that experience if that particular person hadn't been there?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	So did that ruin it for you really, or..?

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	How was it resolved in the end? Did you go to somebody?

Subject:	Oh, I went to his line manager because I wasn't taking it – him standing there accusing me of something I hadn't done and he was. The unfortunate thing was that transportation and geotechnics were right next to each other so I still had to see him every day. You know, that's just one of those things – it does happen.

Interviewer:	Was the company actually quite supportive? They were happy to move you?

Subject:	They were happy to move me, but the (?) recommended that I didn't go back to them, which is a bit of a shame.

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think that is what – that might have been combined with being ill, why they got – why they were happy to terminate sponsorship course – that was just because you were ill?

Subject:	Er, I think there were several factors in terminating the sponsorship. Erm, not least that a new person took over HR and the company was in financial difficulty, that they were trying to cut down on sponsored students. Erm, it certainly didn't help that I had to take a break (Yeah). Erm, and I probably did contribute that I shouldn't go back there. Yeah, I'm not sure exactly why they reached that decision. They obviously thought I wasn't doing my work or something – but to my knowledge I did everything that was asked of me, and, you know there's – you can't do more when you aren't really part of the team. It's when you don't actually know the whole picture of what's going on, you know, you have to stick to what you've been told to do.

Interviewer:	Yeah, what do you think are like the advantages and disadvantages of having sponsorship?

Subject:	Well, the advantages are that you are linked to a company, from the start. And you obviously receive financial support and you know, you can go out for your industrial placement without having to worry about finding a job. And then you go into a job at the end of it. So on the whole it's a good thing. Plus, you know, if you need help for something – you know, you just need to send an email to your company and they'll come back with whatever you need. They'll just get it.

Interviewer:	Did you have to pay the money back that they'd given you?

Subject:	No, well, I think it's only one company that does that because legally they can't do that. (Right). Only one company's very clever, they basically call you a part-time employee and it's wages.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the whole sort of educational experience, and the way that you're taught reflects at all what it's like in industry?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it should do more?

Subject:	Well not really because we're here to learn the knowledge that we need, out in industry. We're not here to learn what it's like in industry because we'll learn that when we get to that part. It's more important, at this stage, to accumulate the knowledge that you're going to need and become a competent person, you know, in whatever area you're going to specialise in.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you know what type of company you'd like to work for when you finish?

Subject:	Erm, well at the moment I'm debating whether or not to go into engineering. If I do then I would need to work for a consultancy because as I mentioned, I'm married and I couldn't really work for a contractor and move around the country, at a moments notice. I certainly need to stay in one place and have fairly – well a choice, either sort of set working hours or flexible working hours but not sort of over long working hours.

Interviewer:	Yeah, not we need you here, now?

Subject:	So I'm just going to wait and see, and decide nearer the time whether I'll just go into engineering or not.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of factors do you think will influence your decision?

Subject:	Well the fact that you can't really go into engineering and take time out to have a family.

Interviewer:	Is that quite a big issue? Why?

Subject:	Because you – engineering is such that you – that you have to keep abreast of all the changes going on and that you know, if you leave, for say 10 years, you know while you have kids and you know they grow up and go to school, and then you try and go back, they might re-employ you but you're not going to be where you were before. They'll stick you somewhere lower although I'm not sure if legally they're allowed to do that any more, because I think that might just have changed.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the companies should do more to try and accommodate women and people with families?

Subject:	Well, the problem is that women are either willing to put their children into nurseries, in which case there's not really a problem, except that they should be allowed you know, whatever time off they need to attend to the child, erm, or, you know the other side of the coin is when – like me – who are not going to put their children in nurseries because they've seen what nurseries are like. Erm, you know, I think there should be ways of getting back in to where you were. I don't know how. It should be possible somehow.

Interviewer:	What skills do you think that you'll take from the course into the workplace? Do you think you've learnt – especially if you don't go into engineering I suppose – do you think that the skills you have learnt aren't just technical skills?

Subject:	Well, as I mentioned before you learn a lot about group work, you know when I was like dealing with people, you wouldn't necessarily choose to work with. Erm, on the MEng stuff certainly we learnt leadership skills and the sort of managerial side of things. Erm I mean basically we learnt how to allocate your work, how to distribute time, how to get everything done within set limits and that's valuable in any job.

Interviewer:	How do you think work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Within an engineering job?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	In what sense? In the work load or…?

Interviewer:	Well yeah. I think you mentioned a bit about that earlier, that you probably felt that work wouldn't be as hard as doing the degree but maybe in how you're treated and what is expected of you?

Subject:	Well, I think coming from university, you learn how to meet deadlines which is always valuable to industry. Erm, and you also learn to meet your targets. I'm trying to think. 

Interviewer:	That's OK.

Subject:	Can you re-phrase the question?

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university experience prepares you at all for going into industry?

Subject:	I think so. I think it does because when it comes down to it university's a sort of mixed bunch of people and industry's a mixed bunch of people and I don't know it's just what I said before really. I mean you learn how to do your work efficiently and you learn how to deal with the pressure, and that's something you do learn, at university, that you will need. You learn how to deal with stress – what to do when there are people around you and you feel stressed.

Interviewer:	Going back to the placement again. Were the university very helpful in trying to find you a local placement?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Did you think that they did everything they could?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean like basically we know it's up to us to get a placement if you want one, and if we want one, there is a placement out there for us. Erm, you know, provided you can travel basically. The problem is that there aren't very many civil engineering companies in this area, and of course, those that have sponsored students here who'll be taking the sponsored students on, and they may not have space for other students. But we have a person, in the department, who co-ordinates. You know, companies come to him and say well, we've got a vacancy, can you tell your students – so we'll find out about any company that's looking for somebody and we also have employer presentations where civil engineering companies come into the department and basically advertise whatever placements they've got going.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there's anything else that they could have done or were you satisfied with what they did?

Subject:	Well, short of going and getting a job for me, they've done everything they could do.

Interviewer:	OK, that's fine. Moving on a bit then, in terms of your career where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	 (lost words) I'm not sure at the moment. This is something that's under sort of debate. I may be being a career person doing a job of some description, either in engineering or civil service is one thing. In which case I'll be working really hard and trying to get as far as I can as quickly as I can. Erm, or it may be that, you know, we've decided that [husband's] going to work and that I'll stay at home and have children. So we're gonna wait and see and well, it depends on what happens and what opportunities arise.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that if you do go to work, you said about climbing the ladder, that you would want to go into like a management role?

Subject:	Yes. Yeah, I wouldn't be happy – I couldn't see myself, at 60 years old, sitting at the bottom of the rating. I could not be that. I'm too ambitious for that really. You know I'd have to go into a job that has got some sort of future prospects or I can climb a ladder of sorts. You know you can apply for jobs where you've got fast stream – sort of get into managerial roles, which appeals to me because it's quite challenging and it's the sort of thing that I'm interested in.

Interviewer:	OK, will you be looking into things where that will allow you to take time out to have a family, or, if you decide to have a family will you do that first and then think about having a career?

Subject:	Erm, again I just – at the moment I don't know. There's every chance that if I decide to go for it, it'll be that my husband will stay at home and look after the children, because he wants to start up his own business, which would be ideal. Erm, but that does depend on me getting a good job – you know something that I'm interested in that I can keep on going for the next 40 years.

Interviewer:	So what would be the ideal career for you?

Subject:	Oh well, at the moment the civil service is very appealing – going into the foreign service and you know, they do a fast stream thing and it's used for…

Interviewer:	I applied for the civil service (have you?) Yes.

Subject:	Have you heard from them?

Interviewer:	No, not now but before (oh right) before – actually when I was doing my Masters I applied to them and I got through the first stage but didn't get through the second stage.

Subject:	Yeah, this is what I find slightly disturbing that I probably won't get through, and then I'm back to square one. But I've read the notes I have to have a keen political interest. So I'm going to be reading up on my politics over the next 18 months, which will be fun. But I briefly worked, as a civil servant, you know for several months while I was out of Uni. I was working for a valuation office, which is sort of Inland Revenue type stuff and that's civil service. So if they can write me a reference I'll be fine.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think is the main barrier between you and getting into the civil service?

Subject:	Their application process. (Yes) You know, if I could meet one of the managers and speak to them I'd be fine but it's the filling in of computer forms that really is quite daunting, because you have to say the right thing in – you have to use the right words and if you don't – you know you're out of it before you've started.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? If you went back to the start would you do anything differently?

Subject:	Erm, probably not actually. I don't think so. I'd probably still be sitting here right now.

Interviewer:	Even the bad things that have happened – do you feel like you've learnt from them?

Subject:	Yeah, I wouldn't go back and change them. I think you know – the situation when I was working for 3 months, I could probably have handled that better. You know, and I've learnt from that so I wouldn't go back and change it. You know if I'd been slightly wiser, I feel I could have avoided that situation from happening, but I didn't. You know I just let it drift until it came to a head, so yeah.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Give me an example of a characteristic.

Interviewer:	Adjectives really. Would you describe it as male dominated or intense or traditional?

Subject:	Erm, is this the construction industry?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Erm...

Interviewer:	If you can't think of 5 that's fine. I think I've only had one person that's thought of 5.

Subject:	Well it's long hours, erm, you need to be committed, what's another thing? (long pause) Poorly paid (laughs) I'm not sure on that.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is a masculine industry?

Subject:	Oh very much so. Undoubtedly. That's half the reason I'm doing an MEng, that way I can get out and they'll go 'what did you do, oh you did European studies? Oh that's very nice, I did civil engineering.' Not really, but you know.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will stay like that or do you think it will get better?

Subject:	No, it'll stay like that.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is?

Subject:	Because there are a lot of men and although there are some women out there who you know, want to go and play in the mud and enjoy surveying all day long and all the rest of it, most women don't and that's because of fundamental differences between men and women. And, you know, this whole family issue (yeah) and unless, that's you know, resolved thoroughly – and even then there won't be any sort of equality, in terms of you know equal number of men and women because women don't want to do engineering.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact women don't want to do engineering is a bigger issue than men not accepting women in the industry?

Subject:	No, I think women will be more accepted in the industry, I just think that the numbers won't increase.

Interviewer:	It'll never be 50/50?

Subject:	No, because although women – the women that go into it, are very good at it. You know whereas as I said men just drift into it, I mentioned that, erm but it's not going to be 50/50 because women aren't stupid enough to want to work, you know from six in the morning until seven at night in a mud pit. That's like in very general terms and you know there are women that'll do it – generally speaking, its not going to happen.

Interviewer:	OK, that's everything thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I'll start off telling you a bit about what we're doing, so the bigger picture makes sense to you. We're looking at women engineering students' first experience of the workplace (uh huh) and we're seeing what impact it has on their career (right) which is mainly why we want to interview people that are going on placement, but we're also asking questions about the first educational experiences of engineering and expectations, and also why women have chosen not to go on placement or aren't going on placement, so that's why we wanted some non-placement students. And at the end of the project we're going to put some guidelines together and we'll give them back to the engineering industry. So I'll start off just asking you about some background questions and about why you wanted to do engineering – is it civil engineering you're doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm trying to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you doing the Masters course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What A levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I did general studies, German, and maths and physics.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Now you're asking. It was a – it's got a special name and I can't remember. It was basically a local comprehensive but it's an ecumenical school with a church entry requirement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right OK

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But it's 11 to 18.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Boys and girls?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I did do 3 months with [company] in [town] but that was at the end of my first year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Are either of your parents engineers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So when and why do you think that you decided to study engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I was originally interested in geo physics, erm sort of working with volcanoes or earthquakes but because geo physics has a very narrow qualification I decided that civil engineering would be better. Because – although it would allow me to do geo physics if I wanted to – you know I could specialise in that, it would also enable me to take on other jobs if, you know, over the 4 years, I decided that I wanted to do something else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK did you decide to do engineering before you chose your A levels, or after?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: After.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide which 'A' levels to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well it was based on the subjects I found interesting and that I was good at.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK did anything else influence your decision to study engineering, like parents or anything in the media, or careers advice – anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably my mum because my uncle studied civil engineering and so I think my mum originally suggested it, because I hadn't really heard much about engineering. It was sort of something that existed in the sub-conscious somewhere – you don't really actively think about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – did you do much career research then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh my goodness, I did an awful lot but I can't say engineering ever came up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you talk to your uncle about engineering then – did he encourage you or discourage you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, my uncle did a BEng in civil engineering and then went into the finance world. So I didn't really talk to him about it no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider doing any of the other types of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes, I applied for both aero and civil but I decided to go with civil because I dec – well, aero has an element of electronics in it and I cannot do electronics. And in the end I decided that civils was probably more diverse and that I would find it more interesting in the long run.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's great, how did you decide to come to [university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well my maths teacher came here and that was the first I'd heard about it. Mm, it – my choice was really between [this university] or [university 2], because they both have very good civil engineering and aero eng departments. And, in the end I decided [this university], because I came here for a visit and it was friendly – [university]. And yeah, [university 2] actually has got a big hill, so you've got the halls of residence on the top and the civil engineering department at the bottom and I just really didn't fancy that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I don't blame you! When you decided to do civil engineering then, did you realise it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I mean my maths 'A' level was – well the mechanics group it was 9 boys and me – so, it didn't really phase me at all and a lot of my friends are male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to be engineers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I think – well, I felt that – you know – it wasn't really given to me as an option when I was at school. I knew virtually nothing about it. And I don't know what the case was for the boys – you know, maybe they knew about it – just sort of intuitively or something, er but certainly you know, it wasn't flagged up as something I could do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be done? How do you think they could go about encouraging more women, or making more women aware?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'm not sure (laughs). I've erm, I belong, I've joined WES, you know, I'm sort of doing the – what is it? – the e-mentoring scheme, with the local schools and I think that's probably quite a good way because the girls have teamed up with one us university students and you know, although it's actually just sort of – almost a friendship via email – you know, they can ask you questions about university and about engineering specifically. And they are sort of between 11 and 14 I think. So that's quite an early age but not too early to make them aware that there is this thing called engineering out there. Which is a good thing – but obviously that's only – that only reaches a very small number of people. You know, probably the best thing would be to address 'A' level students who are doing maths and/or physics. Or just general careers sense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What sort of an engineer?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh a civil engineer.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A civil engineer. Erm, ability to work in mud (laughter). You've got to be determined and, to get anywhere, you need to be ambitious. So you have to – even when you've finished university – you have to carry on working towards your chartered status, so you need to be willing to put in the extra work that's required and not expect a 9 to 5 job. So if you want to rise in the company, you need to put in probably about 110%. You know, so people can see you're there, see you're dedicated and that you're making the effort. Erm, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male ones – in there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, no because women that choose to go into engineering usually know what they're up against and whereas men appear to sort of drift into engineering for lack of anything else to do, women actually choose to do engineering and will only do – you know they know they're good at it and its something they're interested in. So in a strange way, those characteristics possibly apply more to women than men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a female engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it's a disadvantage when you're starting out, because like it or not, many men are still prejudiced and you know, although they'll have women in their working team and they'll be used to working with them, when a new woman turns up – you know – it's a case of sort of getting to know them and until you know the way they do the job, they're sort of possibly more on probation than the men would be. And you're sort of – well, when I was working anyway, I felt I had to put in extra effort above and beyond what I was actually asked to do – you know – in order to be accepted. And I'm not sure that would apply to men. But then, later on, you know if you're a manager, as a woman, and your team happen to be men, then you've got an awful lot of control because women are probably more manipulative – aren't they? You can probably get them to do more, than if there was a male on the job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. So – but you think it's harder for them to get into that position in the first place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Well, not least because you cannot be an engineer and have a family – it just doesn't work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that worry you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I'm not going to be an engineer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, we'll talk about that later. Has the degree been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In as far as I expected anything, yes, it's always hard work. I don't think I really had any firm expectations before I came. I'd read the course content and I knew vaguely what we would be attacking but erm….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about in terms of the gender proportions or the type of teaching that you've had?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The teaching's been very good – actually with probably one or two exceptions. The teaching has been excellent. Gender proportions are fine – it just doesn't fuss me at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many women are on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, in this year er I think 10 women and 64 in total, so 54 men. And from my other year, I think there were only 5 women and 70 men – that was when we started, I think since then a few have dropped out but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What has been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I'm not sure really. The best thing is getting course work in on time – in civil engineering we don't have any choice – we have to hand it in otherwise it doesn't get accepted.. The worst thing has got to be the sheer volume of work at times, and the fact that you sort of start a week and finish a week without having actually seen daylight, because you're glued to your desk.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that, that helps you – although it's not nice at times, compared to other students doing other subjects, that, that might prepare you for when you do go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, possibly. I was speaking to civil engineers who are out in industry. Very few of them work in the same way they did when they were students. In fact, hardly any. You know, mostly they're doing a range different things but you're not – you're not working as hard as you were – I mean at university – so in a way, we are prepared. You know we'll go out and suddenly work will be easy but at the same time there's a chance that you sort of feel that – you know – why do we work so hard – what's the point if in actual fact, you're never going to touch hydraulics again! Why did you spend2 years of your life learning it. It's just – it's just one of those things because civil engineering' so broad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Are you pleased that you chose to do this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I didn't want something that was all very samey. I wanted something that was quite diverse. Something that would interest me as much as possible.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you think that they had a different style to male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, the problem is she's not strictly engineering – she's more sort of computers or something or another and it's quite difficult because she sets you – she sets her course work which was requiring that you use your engineering knowledge, and yet she herself didn't seem to know what it was that we were looking for, when we came to ask her questions. And – which makes it quite difficult. She's very organised but then again so is all the men but er…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you think that the female lecturer treated you any differently to the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really because we don't have that much individual contact with lecturers, unless, you know, we're going to ask for help and I think everybody just gets treated the same. I don't think there is any noticeable difference. We're all students when it comes down to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's OK. Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you at all? Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. No it doesn't bother me at all that I've got a male personal tutor. I get on really well with him and so on. You know, he sort of keeps up to date with what I'm doing, which is great. But no, it hadn't even occurred to me that I might want a female personal tutor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. Is there anything or anyone that you'd say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Is that in academic terms or…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, or even … ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, in academic terms I don't know – I think friends who are interested in the same thing, who are doing the same piece of work – has been very motivating, because when you get stuck there's always some people to talk to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, that's fine. Has the type of teaching that you've had involved much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: As in course work groups or labs?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Both, yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well we do erm lab work – that's all done in groups. Erm, that's been quite significant amount of work. And then we also have group work, which is course work which to be submitted in groups.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you work in groups, how do you decide who you're going to work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well, there's people that you know and people you know complement your skills, generally when you've got a choice. Lab groups are allocated – so you just do the best you can within that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you tend to work with males or females or doesn't it bother you either way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn't bother me either way. Erm, it just so happened that my lab group was 3 males and in other group work I've been with like another girl and 2 males. Erm, …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that males and females bring different skills to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No, the skills are purely dictated by what personality and the ability of the person, to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You want the details? (yeah) Right, well I worked in a group with 2 of my friends – 2 males, 1 female and it just so happened that I had a personality clash with one of my friends, which we hadn't realised before because it doesn't come into conflict – but we're both leadership types and it was a male, which wasn't a problem but you know, it just so happened, and he was unable to recognise what was going on and to deal with it. So his attitude was to just ride over the top of it. So I decided that as he obviously didn't have a clue, I would take a back seat and just get on with the work. And then it happened that this guy and the girl – they were both working on it, when the other two of us weren't around and they were making decisions. And then, you know, we would find out 'oh by the way we've done this', which wasn't really helpful in a group situation. So basically communication was non-existent and I was left out – you know – in one way or another. You know, they wouldn't tell me there was a group meeting or they'd say, 'oh we've organised a group meeting for Tuesday. Are you around?' And I wouldn't be, because I'd previously arranged something. Anyway, went it came to it, it was peer assessed. They'd marked me right down, which you know, I felt was completely unfair because within the boundaries, that they'd virtually placed on me, I'd done the best I could, you know I'd contributed in all areas, I'd done as much work as I could but they – and the girl and the guy who were being basically control freaks, weren't allocating the work really. They were wanting to do everything themselves. So I came out with a bad mark, compared to the others. That wasn't brilliant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think you'd do if that situation occurred again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well that situation is occurring again, because I'm working with this group for my field course that's coming up, but I think it will be fine because I did speak to them about what was going on and you know, I raised my concerns with them and hopefully now, we'll just settle down to some sort of working pattern and it should be fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the benefits or the advantages and disadvantages of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well the advantages have got to be that when you go out into industry, everything's group work. You're very, very unlikely to do anything by yourself. And you know, invariably you will have to refer to somebody else or gather some information that somebody else has collected and talk with them about what happens. Erm, so it's a very good thing to be doing group work, at this stage, because you learn how to get along when – you know – things aren't quite right and you learn what you have to do, in order to rectify the situation. And disadvantages? There aren't really any I don't think

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how have you decided not to go on a placement – because you were considering … ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I was going to go on a placement. Originally when I started university I was sponsored. (OK) But, I got ill and I had to take 7 months leave of absence in my original 2nd year. So I did 3 months of my 2nd year and then I had to leave because I was ill. And at which point, they terminated my sponsorship – erm, all well and good. Erm, so then when I came back, I had to apply to other companies – which has been fine but I'm restricted because of my husband's – he's doing a PhD and I can't – well I don't really want to live outside of the country – I want to commute every week and I just haven't been able to find a job in the area. So I've decided that I'm better off going straight through and then just getting out into industry one year earlier.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. When you did your 3 months, previously, was that with the sponsored company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it was.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of going on a placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Industrial placement?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think the advantages are that you see what you've been learning, sort of being employed and you – you sort of see how – the sort of work when you leave university, because they basically treat you like a graduate and you assume responsibilities in line with your capability. And er that's a good thing because it makes you motivated to come back, learn the extra bit and then get out there and you know, if that's what you want to do. Or, you know it might show you that actually you don't want to do engineering and that you'd be better off finishing off and you know, doing something else. So it's just like a form of taster of what life will be like after Uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like the 3 months experience that you have had went some way in doing that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it helped discourage me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it? Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I was placed between 2 teams – geotechnics and transportation and erm the guy in charge of transportation, for whatever reason, just didn't like me and he made my life a misery – quite literally. And in the end he accused of me lying and I was rather upset by that shall we say and then they moved me to geotechnics and then everything was fine – you know, I really enjoyed that. But, I think the few weeks that I had with transportation was an absolute misery.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you think that was to do with being a woman or just a personality thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I was just a student – you know I didn't know what I was doing – he could pick on me, which he did.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Just inexperience.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and he'd accused me of revising while I was at work, which anybody who knows me, will tell you that's very unlikely. You know, I'd brought my revision books with me, because I'd revised to and from work, on the train. Erm, but I didn't ever touch them while I was – really I just ,,,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what were the best things about that experience then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, being given things to do – where you start off actually not knowing what's going on, but then, by the end of it, erm you know you're competent in doing that. So in my case I learnt 2 different things – I learnt how to set up a programme that basically simulated roundabouts and traffic junctions and I designed the junction and input it. And it involved learning how the programme worked, which was great because, you know, you could see the end product and what the traffic jams were going to be like. Erm, and then with geotechnics I had to write up a report on erm an airfield they were going to build on, which involves us sort of analysing ground surveys and (?) and various things (OK) That was interesting. Yeah, it's also proving useful now I'm doing geotechnics because we use the same sorts of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you was in the transport department, would you have enjoyed that experience if that particular person hadn't been there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So did that ruin it for you really, or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How was it resolved in the end? Did you go to somebody?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, I went to his line manager because I wasn't taking it – him standing there accusing me of something I hadn't done and he was. The unfortunate thing was that transportation and geotechnics were right next to each other so I still had to see him every day. You know, that's just one of those things – it does happen.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was the company actually quite supportive? They were happy to move you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They were happy to move me, but the (?) recommended that I didn't go back to them, which is a bit of a shame.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you think that is what – that might have been combined with being ill, why they got – why they were happy to terminate sponsorship course – that was just because you were ill?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think there were several factors in terminating the sponsorship. Erm, not least that a new person took over HR and the company was in financial difficulty, that they were trying to cut down on sponsored students. Erm, it certainly didn't help that I had to take a break (Yeah). Erm, and I probably did contribute that I shouldn't go back there. Yeah, I'm not sure exactly why they reached that decision. They obviously thought I wasn't doing my work or something – but to my knowledge I did everything that was asked of me, and, you know there's – you can't do more when you aren't really part of the team. It's when you don't actually know the whole picture of what's going on, you know, you have to stick to what you've been told to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, what do you think are like the advantages and disadvantages of having sponsorship?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, the advantages are that you are linked to a company, from the start. And you obviously receive financial support and you know, you can go out for your industrial placement without having to worry about finding a job. And then you go into a job at the end of it. So on the whole it's a good thing. Plus, you know, if you need help for something – you know, you just need to send an email to your company and they'll come back with whatever you need. They'll just get it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have to pay the money back that they'd given you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, well, I think it's only one company that does that because legally they can't do that. (Right). Only one company's very clever, they basically call you a part-time employee and it's wages.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the whole sort of educational experience, and the way that you're taught reflects at all what it's like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it should do more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well not really because we're here to learn the knowledge that we need, out in industry. We're not here to learn what it's like in industry because we'll learn that when we get to that part. It's more important, at this stage, to accumulate the knowledge that you're going to need and become a competent person, you know, in whatever area you're going to specialise in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you know what type of company you'd like to work for when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well at the moment I'm debating whether or not to go into engineering. If I do then I would need to work for a consultancy because as I mentioned, I'm married and I couldn't really work for a contractor and move around the country, at a moments notice. I certainly need to stay in one place and have fairly – well a choice, either sort of set working hours or flexible working hours but not sort of over long working hours.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, not we need you here, now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So I'm just going to wait and see, and decide nearer the time whether I'll just go into engineering or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of factors do you think will influence your decision?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well the fact that you can't really go into engineering and take time out to have a family.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that quite a big issue? Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because you – engineering is such that you – that you have to keep abreast of all the changes going on and that you know, if you leave, for say 10 years, you know while you have kids and you know they grow up and go to school, and then you try and go back, they might re-employ you but you're not going to be where you were before. They'll stick you somewhere lower although I'm not sure if legally they're allowed to do that any more, because I think that might just have changed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the companies should do more to try and accommodate women and people with families?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, the problem is that women are either willing to put their children into nurseries, in which case there's not really a problem, except that they should be allowed you know, whatever time off they need to attend to the child, erm, or, you know the other side of the coin is when – like me – who are not going to put their children in nurseries because they've seen what nurseries are like. Erm, you know, I think there should be ways of getting back in to where you were. I don't know how. It should be possible somehow.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What skills do you think that you'll take from the course into the workplace? Do you think you've learnt – especially if you don't go into engineering I suppose – do you think that the skills you have learnt aren't just technical skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, as I mentioned before you learn a lot about group work, you know when I was like dealing with people, you wouldn't necessarily choose to work with. Erm, on the MEng stuff certainly we learnt leadership skills and the sort of managerial side of things. Erm I mean basically we learnt how to allocate your work, how to distribute time, how to get everything done within set limits and that's valuable in any job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Within an engineering job?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In what sense? In the work load or…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well yeah. I think you mentioned a bit about that earlier, that you probably felt that work wouldn't be as hard as doing the degree but maybe in how you're treated and what is expected of you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I think coming from university, you learn how to meet deadlines which is always valuable to industry. Erm, and you also learn to meet your targets. I'm trying to think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's OK.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Can you re-phrase the question?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university experience prepares you at all for going into industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I think it does because when it comes down to it university's a sort of mixed bunch of people and industry's a mixed bunch of people and I don't know it's just what I said before really. I mean you learn how to do your work efficiently and you learn how to deal with the pressure, and that's something you do learn, at university, that you will need. You learn how to deal with stress – what to do when there are people around you and you feel stressed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Going back to the placement again. Were the university very helpful in trying to find you a local placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you think that they did everything they could?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean like basically we know it's up to us to get a placement if you want one, and if we want one, there is a placement out there for us. Erm, you know, provided you can travel basically. The problem is that there aren't very many civil engineering companies in this area, and of course, those that have sponsored students here who'll be taking the sponsored students on, and they may not have space for other students. But we have a person, in the department, who co-ordinates. You know, companies come to him and say well, we've got a vacancy, can you tell your students – so we'll find out about any company that's looking for somebody and we also have employer presentations where civil engineering companies come into the department and basically advertise whatever placements they've got going.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there's anything else that they could have done or were you satisfied with what they did?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, short of going and getting a job for me, they've done everything they could do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's fine. Moving on a bit then, in terms of your career where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (lost words) I'm not sure at the moment. This is something that's under sort of debate. I may be being a career person doing a job of some description, either in engineering or civil service is one thing. In which case I'll be working really hard and trying to get as far as I can as quickly as I can. Erm, or it may be that, you know, we've decided that [husband's] going to work and that I'll stay at home and have children. So we're gonna wait and see and well, it depends on what happens and what opportunities arise.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that if you do go to work, you said about climbing the ladder, that you would want to go into like a management role?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Yeah, I wouldn't be happy – I couldn't see myself, at 60 years old, sitting at the bottom of the rating. I could not be that. I'm too ambitious for that really. You know I'd have to go into a job that has got some sort of future prospects or I can climb a ladder of sorts. You know you can apply for jobs where you've got fast stream – sort of get into managerial roles, which appeals to me because it's quite challenging and it's the sort of thing that I'm interested in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, will you be looking into things where that will allow you to take time out to have a family, or, if you decide to have a family will you do that first and then think about having a career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, again I just – at the moment I don't know. There's every chance that if I decide to go for it, it'll be that my husband will stay at home and look after the children, because he wants to start up his own business, which would be ideal. Erm, but that does depend on me getting a good job – you know something that I'm interested in that I can keep on going for the next 40 years.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what would be the ideal career for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh well, at the moment the civil service is very appealing – going into the foreign service and you know, they do a fast stream thing and it's used for…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I applied for the civil service (have you?) Yes.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Have you heard from them?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, not now but before (oh right) before – actually when I was doing my Masters I applied to them and I got through the first stage but didn't get through the second stage.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, this is what I find slightly disturbing that I probably won't get through, and then I'm back to square one. But I've read the notes I have to have a keen political interest. So I'm going to be reading up on my politics over the next 18 months, which will be fun. But I briefly worked, as a civil servant, you know for several months while I was out of Uni. I was working for a valuation office, which is sort of Inland Revenue type stuff and that's civil service. So if they can write me a reference I'll be fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think is the main barrier between you and getting into the civil service?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Their application process. (Yes) You know, if I could meet one of the managers and speak to them I'd be fine but it's the filling in of computer forms that really is quite daunting, because you have to say the right thing in – you have to use the right words and if you don't – you know you're out of it before you've started.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far? If you went back to the start would you do anything differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably not actually. I don't think so. I'd probably still be sitting here right now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Even the bad things that have happened – do you feel like you've learnt from them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I wouldn't go back and change them. I think you know – the situation when I was working for 3 months, I could probably have handled that better. You know, and I've learnt from that so I wouldn't go back and change it. You know if I'd been slightly wiser, I feel I could have avoided that situation from happening, but I didn't. You know I just let it drift until it came to a head, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Give me an example of a characteristic.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Adjectives really. Would you describe it as male dominated or intense or traditional?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, is this the construction industry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you can't think of 5 that's fine. I think I've only had one person that's thought of 5.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it's long hours, erm, you need to be committed, what's another thing? (long pause) Poorly paid (laughs) I'm not sure on that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is a masculine industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh very much so. Undoubtedly. That's half the reason I'm doing an MEng, that way I can get out and they'll go 'what did you do, oh you did European studies? Oh that's very nice, I did civil engineering.' Not really, but you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will stay like that or do you think it will get better?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it'll stay like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because there are a lot of men and although there are some women out there who you know, want to go and play in the mud and enjoy surveying all day long and all the rest of it, most women don't and that's because of fundamental differences between men and women. And, you know, this whole family issue (yeah) and unless, that's you know, resolved thoroughly – and even then there won't be any sort of equality, in terms of you know equal number of men and women because women don't want to do engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact women don't want to do engineering is a bigger issue than men not accepting women in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think women will be more accepted in the industry, I just think that the numbers won't increase.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It'll never be 50/50?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because although women – the women that go into it, are very good at it. You know whereas as I said men just drift into it, I mentioned that, erm but it's not going to be 50/50 because women aren't stupid enough to want to work, you know from six in the morning until seven at night in a mud pit. That's like in very general terms and you know there are women that'll do it – generally speaking, its not going to happen.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that's everything thank you very much.
